name: Tomas Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Tomas, thanks for joining. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the big supermarket on the edge of town, and I do two things. From six till ten I'm a picker for online orders, pushing a trolley with six crates round the aisles, with a handheld that tells me what to grab. Then after my break I'm on the tills or the click-and-collect hatch, handing out the bags I picked that morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the handheld, weirdly, it's like a game, beat the pick time. I'm still not fast though, I get lost when they move the pasta, and I miss substitutions, like sending oat milk when someone wanted almond. What wears me down is the pay, honestly, it's the bottom rate and the town doesn't have many other jobs like it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Freya, she's a hairdresser in a salon in town. In the evenings I fix cracked phone screens and old game consoles at the kitchen table for a bit of cash. I use AI every day, for repair guides, for writing listings, for basically everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, okay. I'd be a bit disappointed, because I really like the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a great tool, just not magic. At work I'd show people how to use it for the boring stuff, like timesheets. Online I'd probably post a few videos of my repairs with AI helping me diagnose faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the money problem stays the money problem. We have about three weeks in the bank, and Freya's chair rent at the salon went up in summer. The repairs bring in maybe a hundred a month, which is the difference between okay and not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the repairs harder, maybe a stall at the Saturday market, and get proper parts suppliers instead of buying one screen at a time. I'd ask the store to train me on fixing the handhelds and self-checkouts when they break, because now they wait days for an engineer. I'd keep the picking job, because it's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I want to be doing something better, not just surviving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take to do the market stall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred for a table, a gazebo and a stock of screens. That's most of our savings, so I'd do it in steps, buying parts as orders come. Freya thinks I'm mad but she'd help with the sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the store wait days for an engineer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the contract's with an outside company, and they cover the whole region. When the self-checkout dies, we lose two tills for half a week. I've literally fixed one by restarting it in the right order, and the manager looked at me funny.

say: AI is a **great tool**, just not **magic**.
I'd show coworkers how to use it for **boring stuff**, like timesheets.
think: The **money problem** stays the money problem with **three weeks** saved.
Repairs bring in about **a hundred** a month, the difference between okay and not.
do: Run a **Saturday market stall** for phone repairs.
Ask the store to train him to **fix handhelds** and self-checkouts.
Keep the **picking job** because it's steady.

fieldNote: Already earns a **side income** from repairs and sees a gap in store maintenance.

His enthusiasm for AI is **practical**, tied to repairs and listings.

steps.text: Rent a Saturday market table for phone screen repairs
Ask the store to train him on fixing self-checkouts
Keep picking online orders on the morning shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first, and robots slower. Okay, that's my picking job with a smarter handheld, then later a robot pushing the trolley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, not a disaster, if you get ahead of it. At work I'd be the guy telling everyone to try the tools. I'd also say the company should train people instead of hiring outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'm in a decent spot. The handheld already plans my route, so it'll just get sharper, and the real robots for picking are a few years off. Meanwhile someone has to look after all the machines, and that could be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an online electronics and robotics basics course in the first few months, and use AI to study along. I'd volunteer to be the store's go-to person for the handhelds and self-checkouts. I'd grow the repair side to two hundred a month and put half of it away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a bit of worry about money while I do all this. Excited wins most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company should train people. What if they don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the regional maintenance company and ask for an apprenticeship. They're always short, the engineer told me. I'd take a pay cut for a year if I had to, which would be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Jun on the hatch, he hates the handheld already and keeps a paper list. He's good with customers though. I'd show him the basics, but he'd have to want it.

say: This is a **chance**, not a disaster, if you get ahead of it.
The company should **train people** instead of hiring outside.
think: I'm in a **decent spot**; the handheld will just get sharper.
Someone has to **look after the machines**, and that could be me.
do: Start an **electronics and robotics** basics course online, studying with AI.
Volunteer as the store's **go-to person** for machines.
Grow repairs to **two hundred** a month and save half.
S1.quote: Someone has to look after all the machines, and that could be me.
fieldNote: Sees **maintenance** as his way up, not out, of retail.
Would accept a **pay cut** for an apprenticeship despite thin savings.
Notices his friend **Jun** resists the handheld and still uses paper.

steps.text: Take an online electronics and robotics basics course
Use AI daily to study electronics faster
Grow phone repairs to two hundred a month
Save half of the repair money each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 for AGI, robots by 2031. That's fast, faster than I'd like even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from government and companies for everyone who gets hit, because it's way too fast for most people. At work I'd say learn to fix the machines, it's the last job to go. Online I'd share what I'm learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think thinking AI will do my handheld planning and the ordering before I blink, and by 2031 a picking robot does my trolley. Repairing robots might last a bit longer, but the AI will tell anyone how to fix them. So my advantage is smaller than I thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the regional maintenance company apprenticeship this year, even on lower pay, because I need hands-on robot experience before 2031. I'd keep the repair business going, but switch from phones to fixing robot vacuums and smart home stuff. Freya and I would cut takeaways completely and live on the bare minimum for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, I'll be honest. The buzz is still there, but there's a clock on it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Freya talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably whether her salon lasts, because hairdressing is hands-on and fiddly. She'd say people will always want a person doing their hair. I'd half believe her and half want her to have a plan B too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI will tell anyone how to fix robots. So why bother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because knowing how and actually having done it are different things. AI told me how to fix a console once and I still cracked the case. Hands matter, at least for a few years.

At work I'd say **fixing machines** is the last job to go.

fieldNote: Admits his **advantage** shrinks if AI can coach anyone through repairs.
Bets on **hands-on experience** as the gap that still matters.
Wants his partner Freya to have a **plan B** too.

steps.text: Apply for an apprenticeship with the regional maintenance company

Cut takeaways completely for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AGI, robots around 2034. That's roughly what I'd guess, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready if you start now. At work I'd push for the store to pay for staff to learn maintenance. Online I'd be positive but realistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's a good timeline for me. I'd have till about 2031 before the planning side changes, and until 2034 before the picking robots, which is seven years. That's enough to get a full maintenance qualification and some experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd do the electronics basics online, then a two-year part-time engineering course at the college. I'd keep picking for the wage, and do repairs on weekends. I'd try to get three months saved by 2028, so I can afford the jump to an apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. Like I've got a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get in the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, always. If Freya's salon has a slow year, we can't both be on lower pay. So one of us has to stay steady while the other moves, and right now that's her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fixing the picking robots in the same store, maybe. Going back to look after the robot that took my old job would be funny. I'd be fine with that.

I'd push the store to **pay for** staff to learn maintenance.
think: Seven years until **picking robots** is enough for a **full qualification**.
Thinking AI changes the **planning side** around 2031.

Keep **picking** for the wage and repair on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. Okay, that's comfortable for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the easy one, there's no reason to be caught out. At work I'd say start now and it's fine. To friends I'd say I'm actually looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine, probably better off. Ten years is long enough to become a proper engineer and maybe run my own repair business. The risk is mostly that money stays tight and I go slower than I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the course over three years at a pace that doesn't break us. I'd turn the repair side into a proper registered business by 2028. And I'd use AI for everything, quotes, diagnostics, bookkeeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, a bit impatient. I want to get going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this one that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that other people get the same idea and the repair market fills up. If everyone retrains as a robot technician, the pay drops. I'd want to be early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Freya say about you running your own business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say do it, she's been self-employed for years with her salon chair. She'd also say keep the shop job until it pays the rent on its own. Fair enough.

I'm actually **looking forward** to it, I'd tell friends.

Register the repair side as a **proper business** by 2028.

fieldNote: Adaptive and **optimistic**, but money still keeps him off calm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd need to jump before I'm ready and we'd have no cushion. What would help is apprenticeships that pay close to what I earn now, so I don't have to choose between rent and learning. Free robotics courses at the college would be great too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who fixes the robots. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, nobody talks about who keeps them running. That's where people like me could go.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, nobody talks about who keeps them running.
portrait: Tomas is 27, an **online orders picker** and till worker on the edge of town.
He lives with **Freya**, a hairdresser, and fixes **phone screens** at night for cash.
He uses **AI daily** and sees **machine maintenance** as his way forward.
Thin savings make the fast AGI picture **nervous**, but longer timelines feel like a **map**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have to jump before he's **ready**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** close to his current wage, and free **robotics courses**.
